Q55347059.summary: Though torn and faded, this silk painting shows a standing, haloed figure with a red moustache and beard, a cross in his headdress, another hanging from his necklace and a third atop the long staff he holds, his right hand raised in a gesture borrowed from Buddhist art. Found in the sealed 'Library Cave' at the Buddhist cave temples of Mogao, it has been interpreted as Christ or a Christian saint of the Church of the East, the Syriac-speaking church that reached China in the seventh century. It is a rare and moving witness to the Gospel's journey along the Silk Road.
facts: The painting was recovered by the explorer and archaeologist Aurel Stein from Cave 17, the Library Cave, which had been sealed around the early eleventh century.
Christian missionaries of the Church of the East, led by a monk named Alopen, reached the Tang capital Chang'an in 635, as recorded on the famous Xi'an Stele of 781.
The figure's three-quarter pose and hand gesture closely resemble Chinese bodhisattva paintings, showing how Christian imagery adapted to its local artistic setting.
Some scholars have proposed that the figure represents Jesus himself; the fragmentary condition makes certainty impossible.
Q55347059.notes: Identification uncertain: the figure may be Christ or a Christian saint. Much of the detail described in sources (beard, crosses) is hard to see in this heavily damaged photograph. Scripture omitted because the subject is not certain.

cur:catacombs-louvre-livia-primitiva.summary: Between bands of strigils, a simple incised panel names Livia Primitiva, who died aged 24 years and 9 months, and below it shows the Good Shepherd with a sheep on his shoulders between two others, accompanied by a fish and an anchor. Modest as it is, it is one of the earliest objects to declare its owner's Christian faith openly.
facts: Its inscription records that Livia Nicarus made it for her sister Livia Primitiva.
Commons notes that the Good Shepherd, the fish and the anchor together show that the deceased belonged to the Christian community.
cur:catacombs-louvre-livia-primitiva.notes: The Good Shepherd is a symbolic image of Christ; here the fish and anchor make the Christian reading clear.

cur:catacombs-arles-paulus-geminus.summary: Three arches on columns frame the scene: at the centre Christ, bearded and nimbed with a cross above, stands with arms outstretched, while two apostles approach from either side, one carrying a cross. Reused as an altar front, the sarcophagus still sets Christ in glory above the altar.
facts: It was made for Paulus Geminus, administrator of the treasury of the Five Provinces of Gaul, according to the Commons description.
It now supports the altar of the Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre in the former cathedral of Saint-Trophime.
cur:catacombs-arles-paulus-geminus.notes: The central figure's identification as Christ is clear from the cross; the side figures are probably Peter and Paul.

cur:manuscripts-grandval-bible-apocalyps.summary: In the upper register, the Lamb and the Lion of Judah approach an altar on which lies the book sealed with seven seals, while the four evangelist symbols look on from the corners. Below, an old enthroned figure has a veil lifted from his head by the evangelist symbols. Christ appears as the Lamb who alone is worthy to open the book.
facts: The British Library's description identifies the scene as the book 'sealed with seven seals' on an altar being opened by the Lamb and the Lion of Judah.
The unveiled figure in the lower register is usually interpreted as Moses, his veil removed by the Gospels — an image of the Old Law revealed through Christ.

links.label: British Library Catalogue of Illuminated Manuscripts: Moutier-Grandval Bible

cur:manuscripts-grandval-bible-apocalyps.notes: Christ is represented symbolically as the Lamb. The interpretation of the lower figure as Moses is the usual one but not stated on the source.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-78-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, with spear and shield, stands in a mandorla and commands a band of angels who hurl spears, arrows, tridents and firebrands at the heathen who have 'defiled thy holy temple' and 'laid Jerusalem on heaps'. In the foreground the walled city bears an idol on its ramparts, and within it the psalmist and his people lament. The lament for Jerusalem becomes a scene of divine rescue.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-78-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-cleansing-temp.summary: Before the Temple building Christ raises a whip of cords and drives out the merchants, who flee before him with their goods. The energy of the scene contrasts with the calm frontal images elsewhere in the book.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-cleansing-temp.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 244); verify against the foliation on the page.

cur:objects2-cma-book-reliquary-cana.summary: At the heart of this jewelled reliquary, shaped like a precious book cover, is an Ottonian ivory of about 1000 telling the story of Christ's first miracle at Cana in three scenes: the Virgin tells Christ and his apostles that the wine has run out; the bridal couple and their guests sit at table; and servants pour water into the stone jars while Christ addresses his mother and the bride. A Gothic goldsmith later set the ivory in a frame of gilded silver and gems.
facts: The museum notes that the reliquary was likely commissioned by Otto the Mild, Duke of Saxony (reigned 1318–48), around 1340.
It was made to contain a leaf from each Gospel and relics of the 11,000 Virgins and other saints, kept in a cavity behind the ivory.
It belongs to the Guelph Treasure, the church treasure of Brunswick Cathedral dispersed in the 20th century.

vam:O88288.summary: In the upper scene Christ rides into Jerusalem on an ass, followed by two disciples, while the people of the city, waving palm branches, spread their garments on the ground before him. Below, he sits at table with his apostles in the house of Simon as a woman kneels to anoint his feet, the meal laid out on a draped table between them. The deeply carved, animated figures are characteristic of the later Metz ivories.
facts: The back of the plaque carries an earlier carving, probably made in the Alto Adige/South Tyrol in the late 8th or early 9th century, with the Baptism and Ascension of Christ; it was cut down at the top, losing the figure of Christ in the Ascension, when the Metz scenes were carved.
The V&A relates the earlier side stylistically to a diptych in the Musée de Cluny in Paris and to a plaque of Christ in Majesty in the Bayerisches Nationalmuseum, Munich.
It was formerly in the Soltikoff collection (sale 1861) and was bought from the Webb collection.
vam:O88288.notes: The V&A identifies the woman as Mary Magdalene. Obverse: Metz, ca. 870–880; reverse: probably Alto Adige, late 8th–early 9th century.

walters:45.13.summary: This tiny silver medallion, under two centimetres across, is framed by a beaded rim with a small tab for attachment. The side shown in the photograph bears a nielloed bust of the Virgin, veiled and frontal, with letters of her monogram at either side. According to the museum's title, the medallion also carries an image of Christ Pantokrator, presumably on the other face.
facts: The Walters dates the medallion to the 10th century; it measures about 1.9 × 2 cm.
It was given to the museum in 1941 by the Baltimore collector Saidie A. May.
walters:45.13.notes: Only one photograph is available and it shows the Virgin; the image of Christ named in the title cannot be seen or confirmed.

Q960157.summary: In Joseph's cluttered workshop the boy Jesus has cut his palm on a nail, and as Mary kneels to comfort him a drop of blood falls onto his foot, a quiet foreshadowing of the Crucifixion. The young Pre-Raphaelite Millais filled an ordinary carpenter's shop with symbols, from the dove on the ladder to the young John the Baptist carrying a bowl of water, presenting the Holy Family with startling realism.
facts: When shown at the Royal Academy in 1850, it was exhibited with a verse from Zechariah: "What are these wounds in thine hands?"
Charles Dickens attacked it fiercely, describing the boy Jesus as a "hideous, wry-necked, blubbering, red-headed boy" and Mary as grotesquely ugly.
To achieve accuracy, Millais painted in a real carpenter's workshop on Oxford Street and used a carpenter's body for Joseph's arms.
The sheep in the background represent the future flock of Christ's followers.
